title: Organizing Your Hacking Workspace 🗂️
description: Structure your projects like a pro so you never lose a script again.

slides.title: Chaos is the Enemy of Hacking 🧹
slides.content:
# A Messy Desk = Missed Vulnerabilities

When you're deep in a penetration test, you don't want to hunt for the right script. A clear folder structure keeps you fast and professional.

We'll create a standard project skeleton that you can reuse for every tool you build.

slides.title: The Golden Project Structure 🏗️
slides.content:
# MyProject/
```
├── venv/               # Virtual environment (already created)
├── src/                # Your Python scripts
│   ├── __init__.py     # (optional, makes it a package)
│   └── main.py         # Entry point
├── data/               # Input files (wordlists, targets)
├── output/             # Scan results, logs
├── requirements.txt    # Dependencies
└── README.md           # What this tool does
```

Adjust names to fit your tool. For a port scanner, you might have `src/scanner.py` and `data/targets.txt`.

quizData.question: Why keep `requirements.txt` in the project root?

options.text: So anyone can recreate the environment with `pip install -r requirements.txt`

quizData.explanation: It documents dependencies, making the project portable.

slides.title: Creating the Folders Manually
slides.content:
# Hands‑On

Open your terminal (with venv active if you want, though not necessary). Navigate to where you keep projects and run:
```
mkdir port_scanner
cd port_scanner
mkdir src data output
```
On Windows you can use File Explorer, but terminal commands are faster and make you look cooler 😎.

slides.title: Create a README.md
slides.content: Every project should have a README. Inside `port_scanner/`, create `README.md` with:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Port Scanner
A simple TCP port scanner built with Python.

quizData.question: A README file is only needed if you publish the code online.
quizData.explanation: Even for personal projects, a README helps you remember what the code does when you revisit it later.

slides.title: Naming Conventions 🏷️
slides.content:
# Be Descriptive

* Use lowercase letters and underscores for filenames: `port_scanner.py`, `brute_force_login.py`
* Avoid spaces; they cause headaches on the command line.
* Name the main script `main.py` if you have multiple modules, or a specific name like `scanner.py`.
* Keep data files in `data/`, results in `output/`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Use Version Control (Git)

Even as a beginner, learn to use Git. It lets you track changes, revert mistakes, and collaborate. Initialize a repo with `git init` inside your project folder. There are great mobile apps for Git too!

slides.title: Your First Script Goes into `src/`
slides.content:
# Let's Place `main.py`

Inside `src/`, create a file `main.py` with just:
```python
print("Port Scanner Starting...")
```
Then run it from the project root:
```
python src/main.py
```
Now you have a working skeleton. Add real logic later.

quizData.question: Given the structure above, how would you run `main.py` from the `port_scanner` directory?
quizData.explanation: Because `main.py` is inside the `src` folder, you must include that path.

slides.title: Workspace Complete ✅
slides.content:
# You're Now Organized

Every hacking project from now on will follow this pattern. Consistency saves brainpower for the actual hacking. Up next: meet the libraries that will turn your skeleton into a beast.
